claims.text: Norovirus is called the stomach flu but is not related to influenza
claims.quote: It is sometimes called the "stomach flu" or the "stomach bug." However, norovirus illness is not related to the flu.

claims.text: Leading cause of vomiting, diarrhea and foodborne illness in the US
claims.quote: Norovirus is the leading cause of vomiting and diarrhea, and foodborne illness in the United States.

claims.text: Symptoms start 12 to 48 hours after exposure
claims.quote: A person usually develops symptoms 12 to 48 hours after being exposed to norovirus.

claims.text: Common and other symptoms
claims.quote: Most common symptoms: Diarrhea, vomiting, nausea, stomach pain. Other symptoms: Fever, headache, and body aches

claims.text: Can feel extremely ill, vomit or have diarrhea many times a day
claims.quote: If you have norovirus illness, you can feel extremely ill, and vomit or have diarrhea many times a day.

claims.text: Most people better within 1 to 3 days
claims.quote: Most people with norovirus illness get better within 1 to 3 days; but they can still spread the virus for a few days after.

claims.text: No specific medicine; antibiotics do not help
claims.quote: There is no specific medicine to treat people with norovirus illness. Antibiotic drugs will not help treat norovirus infections because they fight bacteria, not viruses.

claims.text: Sports drinks help mild dehydration but may not replace minerals; ORS most helpful
claims.quote: Sports drinks and other drinks without caffeine or alcohol can help with mild dehydration. However, these drinks may not replace important nutrients and minerals. Oral rehydration fluids that you can get over the counter are most helpful

claims.text: Severe dehydration may need hospital IV fluids
claims.quote: Severe dehydration may require hospitalization for treatment with fluids given through your vein (intravenous or IV fluids).

claims.text: Stay home 48 hours after symptoms stop
claims.quote: Stay home when sick for 2 days (48 hours) after symptoms stop.

claims.text: Spread routes
claims.quote: Having direct contact with someone with norovirus... Eating food or drinking liquids that are contaminated with norovirus. Touching contaminated objects or surfaces and then putting your unwashed fingers in your mouth.

claims.text: Can get norovirus many times; protection duration unknown
claims.quote: You can get norovirus illness many times in your life because there are many different types of noroviruses. Infection with one type of norovirus may not protect you against other types.

claims.text: Protection against specific types; duration unknown
claims.quote: It is possible to develop protection against specific types. But it is not known exactly how long protection lasts.

claims.text: Older adults and immunocompromised more likely severe
claims.quote: Children younger than 5 years old, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems are more likely to develop severe infections.

claims.text: Norovirus causes inflammation of the stomach or intestines
claims.quote: an inflammation of the stomach or intestines

references.cited_as: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About Norovirus. Updated and reviewed April 24, 2024; accessed November 24, 2026.

claims.text: Most contagious while sick and first few days after
claims.quote: You are most contagious: When you have symptoms of norovirus illness, especially vomiting. During the first few days after you feel better.

claims.text: Can spread 2 weeks or more after feeling better
claims.quote: However, studies have shown that you can still spread norovirus for 2 weeks or more after you feel better.

claims.text: Tiny particles of stool or vomit in the mouth
claims.quote: You can get norovirus by accidentally getting tiny particles of feces (poop) or vomit in your mouth from a person infected with norovirus.

claims.text: Vomit drops spray through the air
claims.quote: Tiny drops of vomit from a person with norovirus spray through the air, landing on surfaces or entering another person's mouth.

claims.text: A few particles can make people sick
claims.quote: It only takes a few norovirus particles to make you and other people sick.

references.cited_as: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. How Norovirus Spreads. Updated and reviewed April 24, 2024; accessed November 24, 2026.

claims.text: Norovirus in vomit or stool before feeling sick
claims.quote: You can find norovirus in your vomit or feces (poop) even before you start feeling sick.

claims.text: No food prep or caring for others until 48 hours after symptoms stop
claims.quote: Do not prepare, handle food, or care for others. Wait at least 2 days (48 hours) after symptoms stop.

claims.text: Especially for restaurant, school, daycare, long-term care workers
claims.quote: This is important if you work in a restaurant, school, daycare, long-term care facility, or other places where you may expose people to norovirus.

claims.text: Hand sanitizer does not work well; soap and water 20 seconds
claims.quote: Hand sanitizer does not work well against norovirus. ... Wash your hands often with soap and water for at least 20 seconds

claims.text: Bleach concentration and EPA-registered product
claims.quote: use a chlorine bleach solution with a concentration of 1,000 to 5,000 ppm (5 to 25 tablespoons of household bleach [5% to 8%] per gallon of water) or use an EPA-registered disinfecting product against norovirus.

claims.text: Leave bleach 5 minutes; gloves; wipe; clean again
claims.quote: Wear rubber or disposable gloves and wipe the entire area with paper towels... Leave bleach disinfectant on the affected area for at least 5 minutes. Clean the entire area again with soap and hot water.

claims.text: Laundry
claims.quote: Handle items carefully without shaking them. Wash the items with detergent and hot water at the maximum available cycle length and then machine dry them at the highest heat setting.

claims.text: Heat resistance and steaming
claims.quote: Noroviruses are relatively resistant to heat and can survive temperatures as high as 145°F. Quick steaming processes will not heat foods enough to kill noroviruses.

references.cited_as: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. How to Prevent Norovirus. Updated and reviewed January 13, 2025; accessed November 24, 2026.

references.record_title: Symptoms & Causes of Viral Gastroenteritis ("Stomach Flu")
references.notes: Older than 5 years but current NIDDK page; content matches 2024-2025 CDC pages; used for patient-facing warning signs.

claims.text: Flu viruses do not cause stomach flu
claims.quote: Although some people call viral gastroenteritis "stomach flu," influenza (flu) viruses do not cause viral gastroenteritis.

claims.text: Norovirus most common cause
claims.quote: Norovirus is the most common cause of viral gastroenteritis.

claims.text: Rotavirus 3 to 8 days; adenovirus 1 to 2 weeks; infect adults too
claims.quote: rotavirus... last for 3 to 8 days... adenovirus... last 1 to 2 weeks... Rotavirus, adenovirus, and astrovirus most often infect infants and young children, but they can also infect adults.

claims.text: Adult dehydration signs
claims.quote: extreme thirst and dry mouth; urinating less than usual; feeling tired; dark-colored urine; decreased skin turgor; sunken eyes or cheeks; light-headedness or fainting

claims.text: Adult red flags (part 1)
claims.quote: change in mental state, such as irritability or lack of energy; diarrhea lasting more than 2 days; high fever; vomiting often; six or more loose stools in a day

claims.text: Adult red flags (part 2)
claims.quote: severe pain in the abdomen or rectum; stools that are black and tarry or contain blood or pus; symptoms of dehydration

claims.text: See doctor if unable to drink enough or not improving with ORS
claims.quote: Adults should also see a doctor if they aren't able to drink enough liquids or oral rehydration solutions... to prevent dehydration or if they do not improve after drinking oral rehydration solutions.

claims.text: Severe dehydration may need hospital
claims.quote: A person with severe dehydration may need treatment at a hospital.

claims.text: Older adults, pregnant, immunocompromised see doctor for any symptoms
claims.quote: Older adults, pregnant women, and adults with a weakened immune system or another health condition should also see a doctor right away if they have any symptoms of viral gastroenteritis.

claims.text: Infants: severe dehydration in a day or two
claims.quote: Diarrhea is especially dangerous in newborns and infants, leading to severe dehydration in just a day or two.

claims.text: Food poisoning definition
claims.quote: When gastroenteritis is caused by consuming foods or drinks contaminated with viruses, bacteria, parasites, or chemicals, this is called food poisoning.

claims.text: Norovirus lives for months on surfaces
claims.quote: Norovirus can live for months on surfaces such as countertops and changing tables.

claims.text: Anyone with dehydration signs should see a doctor right away
claims.quote: Anyone with signs or symptoms of dehydration should see a doctor right away.

references.cited_as: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases. Symptoms & Causes of Viral Gastroenteritis (“Stomach Flu”). Last reviewed May 2018; accessed November 24, 2026.

references.record_title: Eating, Diet, & Nutrition for Viral Gastroenteritis ("Stomach Flu")

claims.text: Normal diet once appetite returns, even with diarrhea
claims.quote: When your appetite returns, you can most often go back to eating your normal diet, even if you still have diarrhea.

claims.text: Restricted diet does not help; no fasting
claims.quote: Research shows that following a restricted diet does not help treat viral gastroenteritis. Most experts do not recommend fasting or following a restricted diet

claims.text: Foods that may worsen diarrhea
claims.quote: drinks with caffeine... foods that are high in fat, such as fried foods, pizza... drinks containing large amounts of simple sugars, such as sweetened beverages and some fruit juices. milk and milk products

claims.text: Lactose trouble up to a month or more
claims.quote: Some people recovering from viral gastroenteritis have problems digesting lactose for up to a month or more afterwards.

references.cited_as: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases. Eating, Diet, & Nutrition for Viral Gastroenteritis (“Stomach Flu”). Last reviewed May 2018; accessed November 24, 2026.

claims.text: ORS first-line for mild to moderate dehydration incl. vomiting
claims.quote: Reduced osmolarity oral rehydration solution (ORS) is recommended as the first-line therapy of mild to moderate dehydration in infants, children, and adults with acute diarrhea from any cause (strong, moderate), and in people with mild to moderate dehydration associated with vomiting

claims.text: IV fluids for severe dehydration, shock or altered mental status and failed ORS, or ileus
claims.quote: Isotonic intravenous fluids such as lactated Ringer's and normal saline solution should be administered when there is severe dehydration, shock, or altered mental status and failure of ORS therapy (strong, high) or ileus (strong, moderate).

claims.text: Replace ongoing losses with ORS until diarrhea and vomiting resolve
claims.quote: Replace ongoing losses in stools from infants, children, and adults with ORS, until diarrhea and vomiting are resolved (strong, low).

claims.text: Resume usual diet during or after rehydration
claims.quote: Resumption of an age-appropriate usual diet is recommended during or immediately after the rehydration process is completed (strong, low).

claims.text: Antimotility/antinausea once hydrated, not a substitute
claims.quote: Ancillary treatment with antimotility, antinausea, or antiemetic agents can be considered once the patient is adequately hydrated, but their use is not a substitute for fluid and electrolyte therapy (weak, low).

claims.text: Loperamide for immunocompetent adults; avoid with fever or inflammatory diarrhea
claims.quote: Loperamide may be given to immunocompetent adults with acute watery diarrhea (weak, moderate), but should be avoided at any age in suspected or proven cases where toxic megacolon may result in inflammatory diarrhea or diarrhea with fever

claims.text: Ondansetron in children over 4 and adolescents
claims.quote: Antinausea and antiemetic (eg, ondansetron) may be given to facilitate tolerance of oral rehydration in children >4 years of age and in adolescents with acute gastroenteritis associated with vomiting (weak, moderate).

claims.text: No empiric antibiotics for most acute watery diarrhea without travel
claims.quote: In most people with acute watery diarrhea and without recent international travel, empiric antimicrobial therapy is not recommended (strong, low).

claims.text: Probiotics weak recommendation
claims.quote: Probiotic preparations may be offered to reduce the symptom severity and duration in immunocompetent adults and children with infectious or antimicrobial-associated diarrhea (weak, moderate).

claims.text: Norovirus pattern: vomiting and nonbloody diarrhea 2 to 3 days or less
claims.quote: Vomiting and nonbloody diarrhea lasting 2–3 days or less | Norovirus

claims.text: Stool testing for bacteria with fever, bloody/mucoid stools, severe cramping, sepsis
claims.quote: Stool testing should be performed for Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, C. difficile, and STEC in people with diarrhea accompanied by fever, bloody or mucoid stools, severe abdominal cramping or tenderness, or signs of sepsis

claims.text: Exception to no empiric antibiotics for immunocompromised people
claims.quote: An exception may be made in people who are immunocompromised or young infants who are ill-appearing.

references.cited_as: Shane AL, Mody RK, Crump JA, et al. 2017 Infectious Diseases Society of America Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Infectious Diarrhea. Clinical infectious diseases. 2017;65(12):e45-e80. doi:10.1093/cid/cix669. Practice guideline.
